front: Why is the demand for health care called a 'derived demand'?
back: Because what people really want is health. Health care is demanded mainly as a means to produce health.

front: What does a price elasticity of demand of -0.2 mean?
back: Elasticity $\varepsilon = \frac{\%\Delta Q}{\%\Delta P} = -0.2$: a 10% rise in price lowers the quantity demanded by about 2%. Demand is inelastic: it reacts only a little to price.

front: Name three non-price factors that affect the demand for health care.
back: For example: health status, income, insurance coverage, time costs (travel and waiting), and information about one's own condition.

front: What does health economics study?
back: How scarce resources are used in health and healthcare, including choices by patients, providers, insurers and governments.

front: Why is economic analysis relevant even when health is described as 'priceless'?
back: Because producing and protecting health still uses scarce resources, so choices involve trade-offs and opportunity costs.

front: What is the difference between healthcare expenditure per capita and healthcare expenditure as a share of GDP?
back: Per-capita expenditure relates spending to population; HCE/GDP relates spending to the size of the whole economy.

front: What is opportunity cost?
back: The value of the best alternative that is given up when a choice is made.

front: What does marginal analysis ask?
back: What happens when one additional unit of an activity, input or resource is added or removed.

front: What is information asymmetry in healthcare?
back: A situation where the parties do not have the same information; for example, a physician usually knows more than a patient about diagnosis and treatment.

front: Why does uncertainty make insurance important in healthcare?
back: People do not know exactly when illness will occur, what care will be needed, how much it will cost or what the outcome will be, so insurance can protect against uncertain financial losses.

front: What is an externality?
back: A cost or benefit from an action that affects people other than the person making the decision.

front: Efficiency and equity: what is the difference?
back: Efficiency concerns how well resources are used; equity concerns fairness in how resources, opportunities or outcomes are distributed.

front: What are the three government roles highlighted in Session 1?
back: Regulator, insurer and provider.

front: Who are the three actors in the medical-care triad?
back: Patient, provider and insurer/government.

front: What is financial intermediation in healthcare?
back: Financing care through a third party, such as an insurer or government, instead of paying the provider entirely at the point of use.

front: Why can total healthcare value be high while marginal productivity is low?
back: Healthcare may create large overall health gains, yet an additional euro of spending can produce only a small extra health gain when many valuable interventions are already funded.

front: Which four broad health-system models are used as a teaching framework in Session 1?
back: Beveridge, Bismarck, American and cash-based.

front: Name the four economic features emphasized when asking why healthcare is different.
back: Information asymmetry, uncertainty, externalities and equity concerns.

front: What does a demand curve show?
back: The quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at each price, holding other determinants constant.

front: Movement along a demand curve vs a shift: what is the difference?
back: A price change causes movement along a given demand curve. A change in another determinant, such as income, health status or the price of a related service, can shift the curve.

front: What is willingness to pay (WTP)?
back: The maximum amount a buyer is willing to pay for a good or service; it measures how much the buyer values it.

front: What is consumer surplus?
back: Willingness to pay minus the amount actually paid.

front: What is a marginal consumer?
back: The active buyer with the lowest willingness to pay at the market price; the marginal consumer receives zero consumer surplus.

front: Name four determinants of how price-sensitive demand may be.
back: Share of income spent on the good, availability of substitutes, necessity versus luxury, and the time horizon such as urgent versus elective care.

front: How can worsening health status affect healthcare demand?
back: People may demand more healthcare at every price; the lecture also illustrates demand becoming steeper when people are sicker.

front: Why can observational estimates of healthcare demand be biased?
back: People choose insurance partly according to health risk, so out-of-pocket prices are not randomly assigned. Unobserved health differences can be mistaken for a price effect.

front: Why are randomized experiments useful for estimating healthcare demand?
back: Random assignment creates groups that are statistically comparable, making differences in use easier to attribute to the assigned price or insurance condition.

front: What are the two major randomized experiments emphasized in Session 2?
back: The RAND Health Insurance Experiment and the Oregon Medicaid Experiment.

front: What broad result do RAND and Oregon support about healthcare demand?
back: Healthcare demand is downward sloping: when the price patients face is higher, use tends to be lower.

front: Is healthcare demand perfectly inelastic?
back: No. The lecture presents healthcare demand as inelastic overall, but still responsive to price.

front: What is arc elasticity?
back: A unit-free measure of responsiveness calculated between two price-quantity points using midpoint percentage changes.

front: What is the full price of a healthcare visit?
back: The monetary price plus other costs such as travel expenses and the opportunity cost of time spent travelling, waiting and receiving care.

front: Why can time costs matter more when insurance is generous?
back: Insurance can reduce the monetary price paid by the patient, while waiting and travel time remain. Time costs therefore become a larger share of the full price.

front: What is a fixed indemnity?
back: A fixed amount paid by the insurer for a particular covered service, leaving the patient responsible for the remaining price.

front: What is coinsurance?
back: The fraction of the healthcare bill that remains payable by the patient; the insurer pays the rest.

front: What is a copayment?
back: A fixed amount the patient pays for each unit of healthcare use, such as a fixed amount per visit.

front: What is a deductible?
back: An amount the patient must pay toward medical bills before insurance reimbursement begins.

front: What policy concern does Session 2 raise about cost-sharing?
back: Higher cost-sharing can reduce healthcare use without necessarily distinguishing between high-value and low-value care.

front: Why does the Grossman model treat health as a form of capital?
back: Because current health is a stock shaped by past and present choices that provides services now and in future periods rather than disappearing immediately.

front: What does it mean to say health is a prerequisite for other activities?
back: Poor health reduces productive time and can limit work, home production and even the ability to enjoy consumption.

front: How do individuals produce health in the Grossman framework?
back: By combining their own time devoted to health-producing activities with purchased healthcare inputs, subject to constraints.

front: What is an unhealthy behaviour in the Session 3 framework?
back: A choice that sacrifices future health in exchange for another goal or short-term benefit.

front: Does the Grossman model assume people fully control their health?
back: No. Choices matter, but genetics, environment and chance also affect health.

front: What does forward-looking behaviour mean in the Grossman model?
back: Individuals consider future as well as current costs and benefits when making health-related choices.

front: What three roles does health play in the Grossman model?
back: Health is a stock of capital, a consumption good that provides utility, and an input into production through healthy or productive time.

front: What is the home good Z?
back: Everything other than health that contributes to utility and is produced using time and market goods.

front: What is the free-lunch zone of the Grossman PPF?
back: A low-health region where an improvement in health releases enough sick time that both health and production of the home good can rise together.

front: Why does the Grossman PPF eventually slope downward?
back: At higher health levels, extra health investment yields smaller reductions in sick time, so improving health requires resources that could otherwise produce the home good.

front: Where is the usual optimum when a person values both health H and home goods Z?
back: On the downward-sloping trade-off part of the PPF, where the highest attainable indifference curve is tangent to the frontier.

front: What changes in the pure-investment version of the model?
back: Direct utility from health is ignored; health is valuable because it creates productive time that can be used for work and other activities.

front: How does the health stock evolve over time?
back: Next-period health equals surviving current health plus gross health investment: H_t = (1 − δ_t)H_{t−1} + I_{t−1}.

front: What is the difference between gross and net investment in health?
back: Gross investment is the chosen addition to health stock. Net investment is gross investment minus depreciation of the inherited health stock.

front: When does health stock decline from one period to the next?
back: When gross health investment is smaller than depreciation, so I_{t−1} < δ_t H_{t−1}.

front: Which variables are stocks and which are flows in Session 3?
back: Health capital H is a stock. Gross investment and the flow of healthy days are flows.

front: What does the MEC curve represent?
back: The marginal efficiency of health capital: the return to an additional unit of health capital in terms of lifetime productive value or utility.

front: Why is the MEC higher when health is low?
back: At low health, small health improvements can release substantial productive time, so the return to additional health capital is high.

front: What determines the user cost of health capital in the pure-investment model?
back: The opportunity cost of funds plus health depreciation, summarized in the lecture as r + δ.

front: What is the Grossman prediction for health and healthcare as people age?
back: Optimal health falls as depreciation rises; the effect on healthcare demand is ambiguous because people desire less health but need more care to maintain any given stock.

front: What is the Grossman prediction when wages rise?
back: The return to healthy time rises, shifting the MEC to the right; optimal health and healthcare demand rise in the lecture's comparative statics.

front: How does education affect health and healthcare demand in the lecture?
back: Education improves the efficiency of producing health, increasing optimal health; healthcare demand is ambiguous because more health is desired but less care may be needed to produce each unit.

front: How does a lower medical-care price affect equilibrium in the lecture?
back: It lowers the cost of producing health, increasing optimal health and raising healthcare demand.

front: What is a health disparity in Session 4?
back: A difference in health — such as incidence, prevalence, mortality or burden of disease — between specific populations.

front: What three broad causal directions does Session 4 consider?
back: Direct causality from SES to health, reverse causality from health to SES, and third factors that influence both.

front: Why does causal direction matter for policy?
back: Because the appropriate response depends on whether low SES causes poor health, poor health causes low SES, or a third factor generates both.

front: What is the efficient producer hypothesis?
back: More-educated people are more efficient at producing health from available inputs, so the marginal cost of health investment is lower and optimal health can be higher.

front: Which mechanisms in the lecture may connect education to better health production?
back: Prevention and risky behaviour, use of information, access to innovation, adherence and self-management.

front: What is the thrifty phenotype hypothesis?
back: Early nutritional deprivation can produce lasting biological adaptations that may become harmful later when scarcity ends, contributing to adult disease.

front: Why are natural experiments useful for studying early-life health shocks?
back: Randomly depriving fetuses or children would be unethical, so natural shocks can create treatment-like and comparison groups without deliberate assignment.

front: What role does the Dutch famine play in Session 4?
back: It is presented as a natural experiment linking in-utero famine exposure with higher adult diabetes and obesity among those exposed.

front: What is the direct income hypothesis?
back: Higher income may improve health because richer individuals have more financial resources and therefore an expanded feasible set for producing health.

front: What distinction does the lecture make between adults and children in the direct-income evidence?
back: Causal evidence for income improving adult health in developed-country samples is weak or mixed, while parental income appears more protective for child health.

front: What is the allostatic load hypothesis?
back: Repeated or prolonged stress can damage health and can be represented in the Grossman model as a higher rate of health-capital depreciation.

front: What is the main Whitehall pattern emphasized in the lecture?
back: Lower-grade British civil servants had higher morbidity and mortality and reported more stressful work and home environments.

front: What is the income inequality hypothesis?
back: Community health may worsen as income becomes more unequally distributed, potentially through social cohesion, stress or political mechanisms.

front: How does the lecture treat the causal evidence on income inequality?
back: It presents associations and proposed mechanisms but stresses that the causal link remains unclear.

front: What is the productive time hypothesis?
back: Poor health can reduce productive time, earnings and labour-force participation, causing lower socioeconomic status rather than only resulting from it.

front: How can childhood health affect adult SES under the productive-time hypothesis?
back: Poor early health can reduce survival, educational attainment and later earnings, creating long-run socioeconomic consequences.

front: What is the Fuchs hypothesis?
back: Time preference is a third factor: people more willing to delay gratification may invest more in both education and health, producing a positive SES–health association.

front: What does a high discount factor mean in the lecture's Fuchs discussion?
back: Greater willingness to value future benefits and delay gratification.

front: What does Session 4 conclude about a single universal explanation for health disparities?
back: No single theory explains all disparities; the lecture presents evidence supporting several mechanisms.

front: What long-run policy emphasis appears in the lecture's final takeaways?
back: Supporting families with children and investing in education may address long-run health and socioeconomic disparities.

front: Why can standard competitive-market models struggle to describe physician markets?
back: Patients face costly search and imperfect information, physicians can have market power, prices can vary, and empirical responses of fees and quantities may not fit simple competitive predictions.

front: Who is the principal and who is the agent in the physician–patient relationship?
back: The patient is the principal and the physician is the agent hired to advise and provide care.

front: Why does physician agency arise?
back: The physician is better informed than the patient and may influence both the information the patient receives and the care demanded.

front: What is physician-induced demand (PID) in Session 5?
back: Physician influence on a patient's demand for care that goes against the physician's own interpretation of the patient's best interest.

front: What is the difference between due and undue influence in the lecture?
back: Influence can support the patient's interest, such as encouraging smoking cessation; PID refers to undue influence on demand.

front: Why do economists model supplier-induced demand?
back: To explain observed physician-market behaviour and to understand how physicians may respond to financial incentives and pricing rules.

front: What does the benchmark model assume physicians value?
back: Net income and leisure positively, while disliking inducement of patient demand.

front: Why can a non-zero level of inducement arise in the benchmark model?
back: Inducement can increase income, but it creates disutility; the physician balances the two at the margin.

front: What is the substitution effect when the profit rate from services falls?
back: Inducement becomes less profitable, creating an incentive to induce less.

front: What is the income effect when the profit rate falls?
back: Lower income can make additional inducement more attractive as a way to restore income.

front: What determines the direction of inducement after a lower profit rate in the McGuire–Pauly synthesis?
back: The relative strength of the substitution and income effects.

front: What happens if the income effect dominates the substitution effect?
back: A lower profit rate can increase inducement and therefore quantity.

front: What role does professional ethics play in PID models?
back: Stronger aversion to inducing care makes inducement more costly to the physician and can limit the response to financial incentives.

front: What does Session 5 say about empirical evidence on PID?
back: The evidence is mixed, but the lecture presents a broad consensus that inducement is not literally zero.

front: Why do PID tests not tell us the absolute original level of inducement?
back: They often test how behaviour changes after an income or fee shock, not how much inducement already existed before the change.

front: Which pure payment methods are listed in Session 5?
back: Fee-for-service, capitation and salary.

front: Which blended payment methods are listed in Session 5?
back: Capitation with fee-for-service carve-outs and case rates.

front: What is the main incentive difference between fee-for-service and capitation in the lecture's policy discussion?
back: Fee-for-service is a higher-powered activity incentive, while capitation is lower-powered with respect to the number of services delivered.

front: What is small-area variation (SAV)?
back: Substantial geographic variation in treatment or procedure rates across nearby populations that cannot be fully explained by measured demand or supply characteristics.

front: What does the practice-style hypothesis propose?
back: Physicians develop different practice styles because knowledge about diagnosis and treatment is incomplete and medical information diffuses unevenly.

front: What is the 'grey area of medicine' in Session 5?
back: Clinical decisions where evidence and guidelines leave room for discretion, with clear appropriate and inappropriate cases forming only small tails.

front: What do the SAV conclusions imply about physicians as agents?
back: Physicians may be imperfect agents not only because of self-interest but also because they can be incompletely informed.

front: What financial problem does health insurance address in Session 6?
back: It protects income against unpredictable medical expenditure that can be rare but financially large.

front: Does the benchmark health-insurance contract remove illness itself?
back: No. It covers the financial risk associated with medical care when the specified illness occurs.

front: What is risk aversion?
back: A preference for certain income over risky income with the same expected monetary value.

front: How is risk aversion represented with utility from income?
back: Utility rises with income but at a decreasing rate: U′(y) > 0 and U″(y) < 0.

front: What is expected income?
back: The probability-weighted average of monetary outcomes: E[Y] = Σ pᵢyᵢ.

front: What is expected utility?
back: The probability-weighted average of utility in each possible state: E[U(Y)] = Σ pᵢU(yᵢ).

front: What is an actuarially fair gamble?
back: A gamble whose price equals its expected monetary value.

front: Why does a risk-averse person reject a non-degenerate actuarially fair gamble?
back: Because the gamble adds dispersion to certain income, and concave utility makes expected utility under risk lower than utility at expected income.

front: Why can the same person prefer actuarially fair insurance?
back: Insurance removes dispersion from an already risky income by transferring resources from the healthy state to the sick state.

front: What is a certainty equivalent?
back: The certain income y* that gives the same utility as the risky prospect: U(y*) = E[U(Y)].

front: What is the risk premium?
back: The difference E[Y] − y*: the maximum expected income the person would give up to remove the risk while keeping the same utility.

front: What three responses to medical-expenditure risk are compared in the lecture?
back: Borrowing after illness, precautionary saving, and pooling risk through insurance.

front: What is the law-of-large-numbers intuition for insurance?
back: In a large pool of similar independent risks, the share becoming sick is more predictable even though each individual's outcome is uncertain.

front: What is an indemnity insurance contract?
back: A contract in which the insured pays a premium and receives a specified payout if the covered contingency occurs.

front: What do p, M, I and π denote in Session 6?
back: p is sickness probability, M the medical loss, I the indemnity or coverage, and π the premium.

front: What is the healthy-state income after buying an indemnity contract?
back: yₕ = y − π.

front: What is the sick-state income after buying an indemnity contract?
back: yₛ = y − π − M + I.

front: What is the actuarially fair premium for indemnity I?
back: π = pI, equal to expected indemnity expenditure per enrollee in the benchmark.

front: Under fair pricing, how do the two state incomes depend on I?
back: yₕ = y − pI and yₛ = y − M + (1 − p)I.

front: What first-order condition determines optimal fair coverage?
back: Marginal utility must be equal across states: U′(yₛ) = U′(yₕ).

front: Why does the fair-insurance optimum imply I* = M?
back: Strict concavity means equal marginal utility requires yₛ = yₕ; substituting the state incomes then gives full coverage I = M.

front: What is state independence?
back: Income is the same whether the individual is healthy or sick; in the benchmark this occurs under full insurance.

front: What is the insurer's expected profit on contract (π, I)?
back: E[Π] = (1 − p)π + p(π − I) = π − pI.

front: How does Session 6 define fair and unfair insurance?
back: Fair insurance has π = pI. In the lecture's technical terminology, unfair insurance has π > pI and positive expected profit.

front: What determines whether insurance is full or partial?
back: The indemnity size: full coverage has I = M; partial coverage has I < M.

front: What is the ideal insurance contract in the Session 6 benchmark?
back: An actuarially fair and full contract for a risk-averse individual.

front: Can a full but unfair contract always be ranked above a fair partial contract?
back: No. The ranking depends on premium, coverage, loss probability, loss size and risk aversion.

front: Which Session 6 assumption is relaxed in Session 7?
back: Session 7 introduces heterogeneous hidden risk types, so consumers can know more about their sickness probability than insurers.

front: What is social insurance in Session 7?
back: Transfers linked to events such as unemployment, disability, ageing or illness; the lecture frames these mainly as transfers across states or time within an individual.

front: How does social insurance contrast with means-tested welfare in the lecture?
back: Social insurance is framed as a transfer within an individual across states or time, whereas welfare redistributes across individuals according to means tests.

front: What is the central second-best trade-off in social insurance?
back: Risk reduction and smoother consumption versus incentive distortions, inefficient behaviour and deadweight loss.

front: Which component of health expenditure creates the basic demand for insurance?
back: The random or residual component, because it makes an individual's future expenditure uncertain.

front: Why does systematic variation matter for insurance markets?
back: Predictable differences in expected expenditure affect premiums, selection, affordability and the distribution of costs across risk groups.

front: What information problem generates adverse selection?
back: Consumers know more about their probability of becoming sick or expected losses than insurers do, or insurers cannot use that information.

front: What is adverse selection in plan competition?
back: More generous coverage disproportionately attracts higher-risk people, raising its average expected cost and premium.

front: What do pL and pH denote?
back: The sickness probabilities of low-risk/robust and high-risk/frail individuals, with pL < pH.

front: What does λ denote in the Rothschild–Stiglitz setup?
back: The fraction of low-risk individuals in the population or insurance pool.

front: What would type-specific fair premiums be if risk were observable?
back: πL = pL I and πH = pH I.

front: What is the actuarially fair average premium for a mixed pool?
back: π = [λpL + (1−λ)pH]I.

front: Why can a full plan cost more than a partial plan for two separate reasons?
back: It pays a larger indemnity and it may attract a higher-risk mix of enrollees.

front: What does the endowment point E represent in yH–yS space?
back: Income in the healthy and sick states before purchasing insurance.

front: How does contract (π,I) move the endowment point?
back: Healthy-state income falls by π, while sick-state income rises by the net payout I−π.

front: What does the 45-degree line represent in contract space?
back: State-independent income, yS = yH, corresponding to full insurance.

front: What is the slope of a type-p zero-profit line in yH–yS space?
Where are profitable contracts relative to a type's zero-profit line in the lecture diagram?
back: Below the zero-profit line; contracts above it generate expected losses for the insurer.

front: Why is the frail/high-risk indifference curve flatter at a common contract point?
back: The high-risk type reaches the sick state more often and therefore values sick-state income more relative to healthy-state income.

front: What are the core Rothschild–Stiglitz assumptions used in Session 7?
back: Two hidden risk types, a static model, no moral hazard, perfect competition, break-even insurers and one contract chosen per individual.

front: How is a Rothschild–Stiglitz equilibrium defined in the lecture?
back: Consumers choose their preferred offered contract and all firms earn zero expected profits.

front: What is a pooling equilibrium?
back: Both risk types choose the same insurance contract.

front: What is a separating equilibrium?
back: Different risk types self-select into different contracts.

front: Why are the symmetric-information first-best contracts not an equilibrium under hidden types?
back: High risks would imitate low risks and choose the low-risk full-insurance contract, causing insurer losses.

front: What transfer occurs in an actuarially fair pooling contract?
back: Low risks pay more than their own expected payout and high risks pay less, producing a transfer from L to H.

front: Why does competition drive out a candidate pooling equilibrium?
back: A firm can offer a profitable contract preferred by low risks but not by high risks, cream-skimming the pool.

front: What contract does the high-risk type receive in a separating equilibrium?
back: Its first-best, fair full-insurance contract with a high premium.

front: Why does the low-risk type receive only partial insurance in a separating equilibrium?
back: Coverage is restricted to make the low-risk contract unattractive to high risks; this is the incentive-compatibility price of separation.

front: What does it mean that low risks are quantity constrained or rationed?
back: They cannot buy the full amount of insurance they prefer, even though they would pay their own fair premium for it.

front: How can a large λ affect equilibrium existence?
back: When low risks are a large majority, a profitable pooling deviation may destabilise the separating menu and the market may have no equilibrium.

front: Why can compulsory pooling improve welfare?
back: It can cross-subsidise high risks and relax the low-risk coverage constraint, allowing both types to reach a better feasible allocation.

front: What policy menu does Session 7 associate with partial pooling?
back: Compulsory basic insurance plus supplementary private insurance, or an equivalent tax on partial coverage and subsidy to fuller coverage.

front: What is premium risk?
back: The risk that a person's systematically expected future healthcare costs and therefore actuarial premium rise after their risk class worsens.

front: What is the main limitation of a lifetime insurance contract?
back: It can preserve pooling but locks people into a long commitment, may be hard to enforce and limits switching and competition.

front: What is a guaranteed renewable contract?
back: A contract with front-loaded premiums designed so both robust and frail consumers voluntarily remain, though switching remains limited.

front: What is the Cochrane lifetime-contract idea in the lecture?
back: Insurers provide premium insurance: a health-status shock triggers a payment that helps finance higher future insurance premiums.

front: What are the three major RS predictions emphasised in the conclusion?
back: Competition eliminates pooling equilibria; separating equilibria ration robust types and make insurance costly for frail types; and the market may fail to reach equilibrium.

front: What is the marginal rate of substitution between healthy- and sick-state income in Session 7 contract space?
back: Along an indifference curve, dyS/dyH = −[(1−p)U′(yH)]/[pU′(yS)]. It is negative because income in one state can compensate for income in the other.

front: How are the L, pooling and H zero-profit lines ordered by slope?
back: Because pL < p̄ < pH, the low-risk line is steepest, the pooling line is intermediate, and the high-risk line is flattest.

front: Why does the pooling transfer balance in aggregate?
back: Each low risk pays (pH−pL)(1−λ)I above own expected cost and each high risk receives (pH−pL)λI below own expected cost; weighting by λ and 1−λ makes aggregate contributions equal aggregate subsidies.

front: What two forces can raise the premium of a more generous plan?
back: A coverage effect—larger indemnity—and a composition effect—the plan attracts a larger share of high-risk enrollees.

front: Write the two incentive-compatibility constraints for a separating menu.
back: Low risk must prefer CL to CH, and high risk must prefer CH to CL: EUL(CL) ≥ EUL(CH) and EUH(CH) ≥ EUH(CL).

front: How does participation differ from incentive compatibility?
back: Participation asks whether a type prefers an offered contract to remaining uninsured. Incentive compatibility asks whether each type prefers the contract intended for it to the other offered contract.

front: What is a cream-skimming deviation?
back: A contract designed to attract profitable low risks away from a pooling contract while remaining unattractive to high risks.

front: What information is disclosed ex post in a separating equilibrium?
back: A consumer's contract choice reveals the risk type implied by self-selection, even though the insurer could not observe type ex ante.

front: Why is solving adverse selection through separation not first best?
back: Sorting is achieved, but low risks receive only partial coverage and therefore bear residual risk; high-risk insurance also remains expensive.

front: How does a compulsory pooling base change the starting point for supplementary insurance?
back: The mandatory premium lowers healthy-state income and the mandatory indemnity raises sick-state income, moving the common endowment from A to a new point G.

front: Why can supplementary private insurance coexist with compulsory basic insurance in the lecture?
back: The compulsory layer creates pooling and cross-subsidy; supplementary contracts can then add coverage from the new endowment while preserving plan choice above the base.

front: What is the long-run institutional conclusion of Session 7?
back: Keeping insurance affordable after people become high risk requires durable cross-subsidies from low-risk to high-risk individuals, which are difficult to sustain without collective or government-backed arrangements.

front: What is the simple indemnity benchmark?
back: A contract pays a predetermined amount when a specified contingency occurs; with one disease and one treatment, a fair indemnity can deliver full insurance in the benchmark.

front: Why does modern healthcare move beyond a fixed indemnity?
back: Many diagnoses, severities and treatment paths make the appropriate expenditure unpredictable before care is delivered.

front: How does Session 8 define appropriate care?
back: Selection from efficacious treatments of the option most likely to produce the health outcomes desired by the individual patient.

front: What is moral hazard in this lecture?
back: Insurance changes behaviour or utilisation so expected loss or healthcare consumption is greater than under undistorted incentives.

front: What is the expected-loss expression used in Session 8?
back: E[L] = p(eP) × L(eL), where prevention effort affects event probability and loss-reduction effort affects loss size.

front: What does prevention effort eP affect?
back: It affects the probability p that the insured event occurs.

front: What does loss-reduction effort eL affect?
back: It affects the size L of the loss or recovery cost after the event.

front: What is ex-ante moral hazard?
back: Behaviour changes before the insured event in a way that makes it more likely; it operates mainly through p.

front: What is ex-post moral hazard?
back: Behaviour changes after the insured event in a way that makes recovery more expensive; it operates mainly through L.

front: Give an ex-ante moral-hazard example from the lecture.
back: Skipping a flu vaccination or neglecting routine blood controls because insurance protects against later costs.

front: Give an ex-post moral-hazard example from the lecture.
back: Choosing a more expensive drug or more intensive treatment when a lower-cost clinically adequate option exists.

front: What three features characterise the standard FFS insurance plan in Session 8?
back: Providers are paid fee for service, insurance lowers patient OOP per unit at use, and enrollees can choose providers broadly.

front: Why can patient and provider incentives reinforce each other under standard FFS insurance?
back: The patient receives extra care at a subsidised price while the FFS provider earns more revenue from delivering more services.

front: Why does moral hazard break the general optimality of full coverage?
back: Full coverage drives the patient price toward zero, increasing use beyond the quantity whose marginal benefit covers marginal cost.

front: Without insurance, where is the efficient quantity in the demand diagram?
back: At Q*, where marginal benefit equals marginal cost.

front: With full insurance, what happens to the private marginal price?
back: It falls toward zero, so the insured may continue consuming as long as private marginal benefit is positive.

front: What are the two determinants of the extent of moral hazard?
back: The magnitude of the price distortion caused by insurance and the price responsiveness or elasticity of healthcare demand.

front: What is the time-inconsistency problem in health insurance?
back: Ex ante, people want a contract limiting low-value use and premiums; ex post, once sick, they want any covered care with positive private benefit.

front: Why can ex-post moral hazard raise the actuarially fair premium?
back: Expected claims include additional care chosen under coverage, so the break-even premium exceeds the premium based only on first-best treatment levels.

front: What does coinsurance k represent?
back: The fraction of healthcare expenditure paid by the consumer; the insurer pays 1−k.

front: What values of k represent no insurance and full insurance?
back: k=1 means the consumer pays the full bill; k=0 means full coverage at the point of use.

front: How does raising coinsurance generally affect utilisation and DWL?
back: It raises the patient price, reduces utilisation and insurer spending, and shrinks the deadweight loss from overuse.

front: What is the risk-spreading versus incentive trade-off?
back: More complete insurance protects income better but weakens price incentives and can increase inefficient utilisation.

front: What is the second-best coverage result when moral hazard matters?
back: Optimal coverage is generally less than full, balancing risk protection against incentive costs.

front: What is demand-side cost sharing?
back: Rules such as coinsurance, copayments and deductibles that make the patient bear part of the cost of care.

front: What is a copayment?
back: A fixed amount paid by the patient per service, visit or episode.

front: What is a deductible?
back: The amount the patient pays before insurance reimbursement begins.

front: What is the main cost of demand-side cost sharing?
back: Greater financial risk and the possibility that patients reduce high-value as well as low-value care.

front: How does price distortion affect moral-hazard DWL?
back: A larger gap between marginal cost and the patient price generally creates a larger quantity distortion and deadweight loss.

front: How does elasticity affect moral-hazard DWL?
back: For the same price distortion, more elastic demand generates a larger utilisation response and larger welfare loss.

front: What is the general optimal-coverage result for inelastic services?
back: They can be covered more completely because quantity responds less to the price subsidy.

front: What is the general optimal-coinsurance result for elastic services?
back: Optimal coinsurance is higher because demand responds more strongly to the insurance-induced price reduction.

front: What is an offset effect?
back: Use of one service reduces use of another service, so greater use of the first can save costs elsewhere.

front: How should substitution affect optimal coverage?
back: A service with large cost offsets on other covered services should generally be covered more generously.

front: How should complementarity affect optimal coverage?
back: If use of one service increases use of another, optimal cost sharing may be higher than when the service is considered alone.

front: What ordering summarises interrelated-demand cost sharing?
back: c**sub < c* < c**comp: lower patient share for substitutes with offsets, higher for complements.

front: Why is interrelated demand hard to address with simple cost sharing?
back: The same service can be a substitute in one clinical state and a complement in another, while plans often set one price per service.

front: What assumption underlies the standard welfare-loss triangle?
back: The observed demand curve accurately represents the patient's marginal utility or willingness to pay for additional care.

front: Why is that welfare assumption fragile in healthcare?
back: Patients may be poorly informed, influenced by fear and anxiety, and delegate treatment decisions to providers.

front: What is Value-Based Insurance Design (VBID)?
back: Setting patient cost sharing according to expected clinical value rather than applying the same cost sharing to every service.

front: Why can preventive care justify very low or negative cost sharing?
back: Patients may underappreciate long-run benefits; subsidies can increase high-value prevention and reduce future costs or illness.

front: Why is healthcare demand partly co-determined by providers?
back: Patients often cede decision authority to physicians, and providers can influence which and how many services are used.

front: What is the traditional view of waste in medical care?
back: Comprehensively insured patients demand too many services, so policy should make users more price sensitive.

front: What is the alternative provider-value view of waste?
back: Waste arises from delivering services with limited patient value, so policy should make providers produce more health value.

front: What is supply-side cost sharing?
back: A plan places financial or organisational responsibility for resource use on providers rather than relying only on patient payments.

front: What defines a managed-care plan in Session 8?
back: An integrated delivery structure linking insurers, provider payment and networks through contracts, restrictions and utilisation controls.

front: What patient risk can supply-side control create?
back: Useful care may be delayed or denied when the plan judges it not cost-effective, even though patient financial risk may be limited.

front: How can a copayment and quantity cap complement each other?
back: The copayment can deter low-value demand first, allowing the quantity cap to be raised for patients with higher marginal benefit.

front: What are four managed-care cost/quality tools?
back: Selective contracting, quality assurance, utilisation review, and gatekeeping or second-opinion programmes.

front: How do HMO, PPO and POS differ?
back: HMO generally uses a network and gatekeeper; PPO uses network tiers without a gatekeeper; POS combines network tiers with gatekeeping.
